chain.g: to pull, draw, tug, pluck off

ety.text: Verb from Middle English pullen, from Old English pullian (“to pull, draw, tug, pluck off”), of uncertain ultimate origin. Related to West Frisian pûlje (“to shell, husk”), Middle Dutch pullen (“to drink”), Middle Dutch polen (“to peel, strip”), Low German pulen (“to pick, pluck, pull, tear, strip off husks”), Icelandic púla (“to work hard, beat”). Noun from Middle English pul, pull, pulle, from the verb pullen (“to pull”).

senses.d: To apply a force to (an object) so that it comes toward the person or thing applying the force.
ex: When I give the signal, pull the rope.
Pull your belt tight before starting off, will you?

senses.d: To gather with the hand, or by drawing toward oneself; to pluck or pick (flowers, fruit, etc.).
ex: to pull fruit from a tree
pull flax

senses.d: To attract or net; to pull in.
ex: Television, a favored source of news and information, pulls the largest share of advertising monies.

senses.d: To persuade (someone) to have sex with one.
ex: I pulled at the club last night.
He's pulled that bird over there.

senses.d: To interest (someone) in dating or pursuing one (whether or not this has led to sex).
ex: Wow, Joyce pulls, actually.

senses.d: To remove or withdraw (something), especially from public circulation or availability.
ex: Each day, they pulled the old bread and set out fresh loaves.
The book was due to be released today, but it was pulled at the last minute over legal concerns.

senses.d: To retrieve or look up for use.
ex: I'll have to pull a part number for that.
This computer file is incorrect. Can we pull the old version from your backups?

senses.d: To obtain (a permit) from a regulatory authority.
ex: It's the contractor's responsibility to pull the necessary permits before starting work.

senses.d: To do or perform, especially something seen as negative by the speaker.
ex: He regularly pulls 12-hour days, sometimes 14.
You'll be sent home if you pull another stunt like that.

senses.d: To copy or emulate the actions or behaviour associated with the person or thing mentioned (with a and the name of a person, place, event, etc.).
ex: He pulled an Elvis and got really fat.
They're trying to pull a Watergate on us.

senses.d: Command used by a target shooter to request that the target be released/launched.
An act of pulling (applying force toward oneself).
ex: He gave the hair a sharp pull and it came out.
She took several pulls on her cigarette.

senses.d: An attractive force which causes motion towards the source.
ex: The spaceship came under the pull of the gas giant.
iron fillings drawn by the pull of a magnet

senses.d: An advantage over somebody; a means of influencing.
ex: The hypnotist exerted a pull over his patients.
Tresham's up to his eyes in dock business and town business, a regular jobmonger, he has no use for anybody who hasn't a pull.

senses.d: The power to influence someone or something; sway, clout.
ex: I don't have a lot of pull within the company.
She wants to work in the villages, and she has a lot of pull with some ministers and there she is, like a political supervisor.

senses.d: Any device meant to be pulled, as a lever, knob, handle, or rope.
ex: a zipper pull

senses.d: A randomized selection from a given set.
ex: card pull

senses.d: A high-quality or funny recommendation by the algorithm.
ex: mythical FYP pull

senses.d: A player's use of a game's gacha mechanic to obtain a random reward.
Something in one's favour in a comparison or a contest; advantage.
ex: In weights the favourite had the pull.

senses.d: Appeal or attraction.
ex: the pull of a movie star

senses.d: A normally regular beat felt when arteries near the skin (for example, at the neck or wrist) are depressed, caused by the heart pumping blood through them; the qualitative nature of this beat.
ex: Her pulse was thready and weak.

senses.d: The rate of this beat as an indication of a person's health.
ex: Her pulse was 110 at 8 a.m.

senses.d: A beat or throb; also, a repeated sequence of such beats or throbs.
The focus of energy or vigour of an activity, place, or thing; also, the feeling of bustle, busyness, or energy in a place; the heartbeat.
ex: You can really feel the pulse of the city in this district.

senses.d: An (increased) amount of a substance (such as a drug or an isotopic label) given over a short time.
A setting on a food processor which causes it to work in a series of short bursts rather than continuously, in order to break up ingredients without liquidizing them; also, a use of this setting.
The beat or tactus of a piece of music or verse; also, a repeated sequence of such beats.
A brief burst of electromagnetic energy, such as light, radio waves, etc.
Synonym of autosoliton (“a stable solitary localized structure that arises in nonlinear spatially extended dissipative systems due to mechanisms of self-organization”).
A brief increase in the strength of an electrical signal; an impulse.
To emit or impel (something) in pulses or waves.
ex: Though a light of love she swimmeth, / Zoned with utterless desire, / And the air of her swift coming / Through thy hot veins pulseth fire.

senses.d: To give to (something, especially a cell culture) an (increased) amount of a substance, such as a drug or an isotopic label, over a short time.
To operate a food processor on (some ingredient) in short bursts, to break it up without liquidizing it.
To apply an electric current or signal that varies in strength to (something).
To manipulate (an electric current, electromagnetic wave, etc.) so that it is emitted in pulses.
To expand and contract repeatedly, like an artery when blood is flowing though it, or the heart; to beat, to throb, to vibrate, to pulsate.
ex: Hot blood pulsed through my veins as I grew angrier.
The streets were dark, and all that could be seen was light pulsing from the disco.

senses.d: Of an activity, place, or thing: to bustle with energy and liveliness; to pulsate.

Edible grains or seeds from leguminous plants, especially in a mature, dry condition; (countable) a specific kind of such a grain or seed.
